Interference. The phenomenon where two or more waves combine to produce a resultant wave whose amplitude depends on the relative phase of the overlapping waves. Waves that arrive in phase reinforce each other in constructive interference, producing larger amplitude. Waves arriving out of phase cancel each other in destructive interference, producing smaller or zero amplitude. Interference is evidence that light behaves as a wave, and it is the mechanism behind diffraction patterns, thin-film colors, noise-canceling headphones, and quantum superposition.

Constructive interference occurs when waves' crests align. Amplitudes add, producing a wave of larger amplitude. Destructive interference occurs when crests of one wave align with troughs of another. Amplitudes subtract, potentially canceling entirely. Path difference determines interference. If two waves travel distances differing by an integer multiple of wavelengths—lambda, two lambda, three lambda—they arrive in phase with constructive interference. If differing by half-wavelengths—lambda over two, three lambda over two—they arrive out of phase with destructive interference.

The double-slit experiment by Thomas Young in eighteen-oh-one demonstrated interference with light. Two slits act as coherent sources, producing alternating bright and dark fringes on a screen. Definitive proof that light is a wave. Diffraction is a closely related phenomenon. When waves pass through a narrow opening or around an obstacle, they bend and spread, a result of interference between different parts of the wavefront.

Thin-film interference, observed in oil on water and soap bubbles, produces iridescent colors as light reflects from the film's top and bottom surfaces. Interference between those reflections selectively amplifies some wavelengths and suppresses others. In quantum mechanics, superposition of wavefunctions produces interference patterns in probability amplitudes. Destructive interference explains why certain quantum transitions are forbidden. The amplitudes literally cancel.

Phase is the key to understanding interference. Waves can be in phase with peaks aligned, out of phase with peaks aligned with troughs, or partially out of phase with intermediate cancellation. Phase depends on path difference. Coherence is crucial for observing interference. Random, incoherent light does not produce interference patterns because different wavelengths and random phases wash out the pattern. Lasers are coherent, so they produce sharp fringes.

In quantum systems, probability amplitudes, or wavefunctions, interfere just like classical waves. Destructive interference explains why certain transitions are forbidden. The amplitudes literally cancel. Waves are the fundamental entity exhibiting interference. Any wave, whether sound, water, or light, can interfere. Superposition is the principle that waves add linearly. Interference is the result of superposition.
